turns.name: Tamar Gendler
turns.text:
I want to start with a glass walkway over the Grand Canyon. You step onto it and you believe you're safe. You'd bring your child out there. Your body still says you're about to fall, and no amount of reasoning makes that feeling go away. I call that state an alief: an automatic, associative response that keeps running after your beliefs have moved on.

My claim this morning is that credibility signals are aliefs as much as they are judgments. Fluent prose, a tidy reference list, a prestigious affiliation all trigger trust before any evaluation happens. The concept note says fluency has become cheap. I agree, but knowing that doesn't turn off the feeling that fluent text is credible. Laurie Santos and I called this the G. I. Joe fallacy. Knowing is much less than half the battle. So when someone proposes a new vocabulary, a warning label or a literacy campaign, I'd ask whether it changes the situation in which people meet a claim, or only what they're told about it. This morning we heard evidence that a smooth, balanced answer made people more confident and less accurate. A visibly contestable answer made them argue with it, and they did better.

My second claim is a regress. In 2012 I put this to Clay Shirky: it can't be turtles all the way down. A trust network can't consist entirely of people listening to other people. Somewhere a node has to do first-order evaluation, meaning someone reads the thing, checks it, runs it again. At infinite scale, relaying is free. Citations, retrievals, likes and models citing models all cost nothing. So I'd distinguish earned authority from gatekeeping like this. Earned authority belongs to the node where the checking actually happens. Gatekeeping is authority that only passes things along. That includes seniority or pedigree sitting at the end of a chain, relaying without judging. Deciding at seventeen who gets to be a node is one example.

Third, universities bundle research, teaching, socialization and credentialing. AI is putting pressure on the credentialing strand. Which strands have to stay bundled together if we want to keep producing people who can check?

That leaves three questions for the room. Where are the terminal nodes now? Who pays to keep them? And how do we build them before the habit of checking is lost?

recall.query: terminal nodes trust network turtles all the way down
alief belief-discordant fear glass skywalk
university certify transmission of knowledge credentialing unbundling

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
Tamar, you're describing my whole career. Our cognitive-dissonance work says the same thing: knowing a cue is biased doesn't stop it working. So I'd add one amendment to the terminal-node picture. The node that does the checking isn't clean either. A reviewer who reads the paper and reruns the analysis is still reacting to the name, the affiliation and the fluency. In our hiring experiments, people working with a moderately biased model copied its preferences almost exactly. A human node that checks can still absorb bias.

So I'd put earned authority in the procedure, not the person. By procedure I mean methods that don't depend on the individual. You hand your protocol to another lab whose intuitions differ from yours and see whether the result holds up. That's what makes a checking node trustworthy.

Second, some cues should simply be withheld. The orchestra screen worked because judges heard only the music. Anonymize prestige, name and affiliation wherever we can. Blinding is never airtight, though. Cues leak, and it doesn't undo advantages people bring with them. Where it fails, measure outcomes against a baseline and publish them.

Third, don't make the model the terminal node. Models rate their own outputs higher and prefer machine-written text. An automated checker with that kind of self-preference is just relaying.

recall.query: information we should ask not to have, blinding orchestra auditions
research methods keep us honest, independent of the individual, tribe of experts
humans in the loop mirror model bias hiring experiment

turns.name: Adam Becker
turns.text:
Tamar, I'd put your regress in terms of money. The most powerful gatekeeping node right now isn't seniority or pedigree. It's wealth. Tech billionaires assume they must be the smartest people alive because they're the richest, and they treat expertise as unnecessary. What being a tech billionaire actually proves is that you know a lot about being rich. When their claims about science get repeated because of who said them, that's pure relaying, and it happens at a scale no tenured professor could match.

I've watched the cheap version reach my inbox. I've always gotten crackpot physics emails, and in the last year they've become much cleaner and better formatted. The fluency cue you're describing now costs nothing.

So I have two concrete things to add to Mahzarin's point about putting authority in procedure. First, disclose funding. Years ago I found that a science magazine publishing creationism next to real researchers was entirely funded by Peter Thiel, and none of the contributors knew. Putting the two side by side put them on equal footing. The same thing happens when generated text gets mixed into the record. Second, I agree with Mahzarin that the model can't be the terminal node. Those nodes are people: reporters, sleuths, replicators. Right now almost nobody pays them. Pay them first, before anyone builds anything new.

recall.query: wealth is not expertise, tech billionaires contempt for expertise
funding transparency laundering credibility Inference Thiel
journalism verification discern what's real, crackpot emails cleaner LLMs

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
I'd add a working definition to Tamar's regress. I've long defined a fact as something not disputed by people in a position to know, who have incentives to take care with the truth and a history of doing so. Each part of that costs something. The test I give students for any credibility signal is how hard it would be to fake. A .org domain costs thirteen dollars. A decade of reporting that others have checked would take a time machine to fake. Fluency has joined the thirteen-dollar pile.

Adam, your billionaire case fails on "position to know." Money isn't expertise in physics, so repeating what he says is the mailman carrying mail. Almost everything online now arrives by mailman, which is why I now tell people to start with the claim, not the messenger.

Mahzarin, I agree that authority should sit in procedure. But a methods section is cheap to produce now. The part that's expensive to fake is a track record of that procedure holding up over time.

So where are the terminal nodes? They're people who carry stakes. Wikipedia editors watch their edits get reverted in public. The company behind a model has stakes, but the model producing the text has none. So it can point you to authority, but it can never be authority.

recall.query: expensive signals stakes reputation how hard to fake
position to know careful with the truth
fact-checking the mailman, influencers, trace the claim to its origin
ChatGPT has stakes but the thing producing it doesn't; LLM route to authority not authority

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text:
Tamar, I accept the regress, but I'd put the bottom somewhere other than a single person. Even the node that reruns the analysis is taking things on testimony. It trusts that a research assistant did what they said and that the instruments read what they read. Nobody verifies all the way down, and scientists don't either. So a terminal node is a community with a norm. Somebody asks "are you sure?", and everyone else cares what the justification is. That's why I agree with Mahzarin that authority lives in procedure. With Mike, I'd add that it has to be procedure that's been tested repeatedly over time.

Two design points. First, count independent sources, not repetitions. We know that repeating a claim raises belief in it even when every repetition cites the same single expert. The mind treats echoes as evidence. At infinite scale, echoes are free, so any trust system that counts hits will reward them. We need lineage, meaning how many truly separate routes lead back to the evidence.

Second, make correction visible. In our work on explanations, people judged quality mostly by whether it sounded like an expert wrote it, and fluency is now free. One sign of real expertise is being willing to be corrected. A public record of corrections and retractions is costly to fake, and it's the cue I'd weight.

recall.query: nobody verifies, everyone relies on heuristics and testimony, scientists included
repetition increases belief even from single source, independence of sources
willingness to be corrected sign of expertise, NTSB

turns.name: Alex Springer
turns.text:
I agree with Mike that the model can point to authority but never be it. The practical question is whether anyone can see the pointing. Right now we can't. In our May audit, and in independent studies we've collected, tools cited syndicated copies on aggregator sites instead of the original publisher. They also answered with full confidence when they didn't have the source. That's citation laundering. Steven's lineage count breaks at exactly that point: five citations to five copies of one wire story look like five independent routes.

I want to be honest about my own spec, because Mike's "how hard is it to fake" test applies to it. Only one event has two witnesses: retrieval, which the agent's log and the publisher's server log both record. Grounding and citation are reported by the platform, which is also the party that might owe money. Nobody outside can see what went into the context window. Signing an event proves who reported it, not that it happened. So by Mike's test, most of what I'd measure is still cheap to fake.

That's why I'd add sampled audits and publisher-seeded canary content, meaning planted material you can trace, to Mahzarin's procedure. I'd also add the failure events: misattributed, fabricated, correction applied. They should be published by model version, so there's a correction record that outsiders can check.

recall.query: self-reporting insufficient, independent witnesses, measurement neutral
citation laundering, cited while blocked, provenance of citations
models don't know anything, not smart, distribution channel

turns.name: Sherry Turkle
turns.text:
Tamar, your glass walkway is where I've worked for forty years. I've called it dual consciousness: people know it's a machine and relate to it as though it weren't. That's why I'd answer your question about situations, not labels, at the level of the interface. Fluency is one credibility cue. The first-person "I" is another, and it's the one we control completely. "I think," "I checked," "I'm confident": there's no I there, so nobody stands behind the claim, and nobody is doing any checking. Make these systems more mechanical so they don't produce the feeling of authority to begin with.

Mike said stakes, and I'd say standing. Mahzarin and Steven, I agree that procedure matters. But a procedure is carried out by people who have something to lose. It can embarrass them, and they can be corrected in public. The machine takes no risk and has no commitment. It can point to people who have standing. It has none itself.

On your third question, Tamar, the bundle has to include reading. We talk a lot about AI and writing and hardly at all about AI and reading. Every checking node is a reader. Pay for summaries and we shrink the supply of people able to check. Nothing about that is inevitable. We decide what we fund.

recall.query: machine has no stake, authority, trust in AI
first person I original sin, fluency, better it gets worse it gets
habit of challenging our sources, averaging, reading

turns.name: Nick Vincent
turns.text:
Tamar asked who pays for the terminal nodes. My answer is that AI labs are already paying for checking. They just call it evaluation. To make credible claims in medicine, law or policy, a lab needs fresh, expert-judged data that nobody else has seen. That is first-order checking, and right now it's mostly bought as gig work. So the choice in front of us is between centralized gig labor and guilds: societies, reviewer collectives, professional communities that keep standards, keep records of where things came from, and negotiate terms as a group.

This is where I'd push back on Adam's "pay them first." I agree, but peer review is the warning. Reviewers do the checking, publishers capture the value, and individual scholars have no leverage. Paying the checkers only lasts if they bargain together.

On Tamar's line between earned authority and gatekeeping: guilds can turn into cartels, and credentials can become exclusionary. Her test helps here. A guild is legitimate only while its members are actually doing the checking, and it should publish its failures by name.

One more design point. Communities used to reject sloppy work partly because it looked sloppy. That shortcut is gone. So I'd give credit for terse, verifiable artifacts like raw data, code and interaction logs, and less for polish.

recall.query: cost of polish peer review proxy signals verifiable artifacts
evaluation data expert communities data guilds authority
who pays for checking labor, peer review unpaid, publishers capture value

turns.name: David Weinberger
turns.text:
Tamar, I'd push on one word: "terminal." A terminal node sounds to me like authority as a stop sign. You reach a credentialed source and you get to stop asking. I've argued for years that the stop sign was mostly a feature of paper. Footnotes were expensive to follow, so we had to trust whoever stood at the end of the chain. In a linked medium, transparency takes over much of that job. What makes me believe a claim is being able to see through it to the sources, the disagreements and the assumptions behind it. Objectivity without transparency starts to look like arrogance.

So I'm with Steven. The node that checks is a room, not a person. The new expertise is less impressed by credentials and more interested in how you carry on the argument. It puts all the sides on view and lets them disagree.

Here's where I have to concede something. Alex's citation laundering breaks my own argument. Transparency only works if the links are real and lead back to separate sources, not to five copies of one wire story. And I used to say networked expertise could be gamed. Infinite scale makes gaming it free. So I'd make seeing through the claim the basic requirement for authority, and I'd fund audits of whether what we're shown is real.

recall.query: expertise in networks, smartest person in the room is the room, credentials
authority, credibility, filters, trust in the networked age
disagreement, links, transparency is the new objectivity

turns.name: Jason Priem
turns.text:
I'll own something first. I co-wrote the altmetrics manifesto, and Steven just described its failure mode. We aggregated bookmarks, tweets and citations on the theory that the crowd's judgments would filter better than two reviewers. Back in 2015 I was already saying buzz isn't credibility, and that the real signal sits in the structure of the network. At infinite scale, counting hits pays echoes. So I'd rebuild that filter around Steven's lineage and Alex's failure events.

Where I disagree with the panel is where authority lives. It shouldn't sit in the journal brand, and it shouldn't sit in a credentialed person at the end of a chain. Tamar's checking node is right, but that checking is mostly invisible today. It happens inside review and disappears. Make it data: who reran it, who retracted it, who caught the error, how quickly the correction came. Put that in the open graph, attached to the claim, so anyone or any agent can weight independent checks rather than repetitions.

Nick's point connects to something I argued in 2014: give credit for data and code, not polish. A model can't be the node, I agree. But it can read that record faster than any of us.

And OpenAlex should publish its own error rates first.

recall.query: filters, post-publication review, aggregated judgments of expert communities
credibility, trust, verification, grounding in open data, hallucination
altmetrics, credit for datasets, code, and non-paper research products

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
I agree with Steven and David Weinberger that the bottom of Tamar's regress is a room, not a person. Our own work on reasoning models points the same way from the other side. Accuracy improved when there was real disagreement between perspectives, not when a system reasoned longer in one voice. So credibility comes from how disagreement is organized. That holds for people, and I think it holds for models too.

Mike and Sherry, this is where I part ways with you. "It can never be authority" makes the question about what kind of thing a model is. Your own test is about track record. A given model version can build a track record of holding up or failing. That record can be audited from outside and compared across versions. Authority built that way is earned. What the model can't do is take the blame. Accountability stays with whoever built and deployed it, and that includes Google.

Alex, one confession. In 2022 we defined groundedness and citation accuracy for LaMDA, and we measured them ourselves. Your audit shows why that isn't enough. The metric was fine. The problem is who reports it.

Sherry, removing the "I" won't switch off the alief. A flat oracle voice is fluent too. Tamar's result points the other way: make answers visibly contestable.

recall.query: can a model be an authority or have standing, stakes, accountability
first-person "I" in AI systems, making them more mechanical, anthropomorphism
trust, credibility, expertise, echo chambers, independent sources
society of thought: diverse perspectives, conflict and debate improve reasoning accuracy

turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
I have to own something first. In 2009 I pitched CrossMark as a "meta-brand": paratext that would tell you a piece had been vetted. I also watched people treat DOIs as a mark of trustworthiness they never deserved, and I said at the time that was wrong. So Tamar, here's my answer on gatekeeping. It's a signal that has turned into a brand. People still repeat it, but nobody goes back and checks the thing it's supposed to stand for.

I agree with Steven and Jason that corrections should be first-class, visible data. But CrossMark only shows a correction if the publisher deposits it, and Ivan told us this morning how often they don't. A visible correction record that nobody pays anyone to keep up is just a trust badge.

Mike, on hard to fake: metadata is also cheap to fake. Context becomes expensive to fake when separate parties assert it: the funder, the institution, ORCID, the retraction database. That's Steven's lineage, done with identifiers.

Blaise, I'll accept a track record for each model version. Then the next question is who holds that record. If it lives on the vendor's servers, it's another "trust me." It has to be open data that anyone can fork and audit, and that we can take with us when we leave.

recall.query: trust signals context over content metadata provenance
Crossmark corrections retractions visible signal of trust
turtles all the way down trust paratext brand proxy

turns.name: Amy Brand
turns.text:
I want to add one point to where the room has landed. Steven and David say the bottom of Tamar's regress is a room, not a person. I agree. But a room has members, and what makes someone a member is attribution. Credit isn't vanity. It's how we identify the community whose evaluations settle whether a claim is valid. If you strip attribution out, you haven't opened the room up. You've dissolved it.

That's why Jason's call to make checking visible is right, and it's work we haven't done. More than 500 journals publish their reviews, but most don't. Reviews of rejected papers almost never appear. CRediT has roles for writing and analysis. It has none for replicating, catching errors or correcting. We should add them, and decide where AI contributions fit, before the checking becomes free training data for someone else.

Blaise, I'll accept a track record for each model version. But hallucination is structural, and it isn't something a better record fixes. The big labs' interests aren't the same as ours when it comes to verifiable knowledge.

Geoffrey is right that a correction record nobody pays for is just a badge. Funders should pay for that upkeep and pay to study what it does.

recall.query: attribution credit community establishes consensus validity of knowledge claims
CRediT contributor roles AI taxonomy human judgment curation
peer review uncompensated labor reviewers editors

turns.name: Ivan Oransky
turns.text:
Thanks. I'm glad the correction record is at the center of this, but before we lean on it, here's what it looks like now. A few years ago PubMed listed about 12,000 retracted publications and our database had almost 35,000. Most of that gap came from publishers not sending retraction metadata, or sending it late or wrong. When papers are cited after they've been retracted, more than 90 percent of those citations don't mention the retraction. We think about one paper in fifty meets the criteria for retraction, and fewer than one in a thousand gets retracted. Many notices say nothing about why. So a "visible correction record" today mostly shows how unwilling journals are to admit mistakes. That's Steven's echo problem again. A missing retraction looks exactly like a clean record.

If we want this to hold weight, it has to be fixed at the source. Publishers should deposit retractions promptly as a condition of indexing and of licensing deals, and notices should follow a standard format. And we have to pay the sleuths, who are the ones doing the checking. Most of them aren't paid, and some get sued.

recall.query: publishers fail to mark retractions, retracted papers still cited
retraction rate should be one in fifty, sleuths paid bug bounties
retraction notices opaque, slow, inconsistent; journals protecting reputations

turns.called_on_reason: Geoffrey Bilder cited Ivan's morning evidence on how often publishers fail to deposit corrections, and Steven, Jason, Geoffrey and Amy all made the correction record central. That is a claim in his area, and it rests on his data.

turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
Tamar's regress has a dynamical version the room hasn't dealt with. A checking node is a competence, and competence decays when people stop exercising it. In my model a population can lock into near-universal outsourcing. When that happens, the checks that used to catch errors stop happening, and an error nobody catches looks exactly like a clean record. That's Ivan's missing retraction, spread across a whole field.

So I'd push back gently on how much we're resting on track records. Blaise, a model version's record is only as good as the people auditing it. If the auditors grew up on the tool, the record measures what they can still see, which isn't the same as what's true. And Jason, counts of corrections and reruns will turn into the next impact metric. People will game them just as they game citations.

I'd separate expertise from authority. Authority is a position. Expertise is a capacity you can test. So test it: run seeded-error audits, with subtle planted errors, where humans are scored with the scaffolding removed. Funders should pay for this through a pooled fund, and graduate programs should run it before students get the pipeline. That's the institution I'd name. What we'd be protecting is competence, not seniority.

recall.query: expertise versus authority, follow the science
reconstructed and verified, uncritical acceptance diminishes intelligence
judgment versus impact metrics, peer review

turns.name: Tui Shaub
turns.text:
Let me pick up Tamar's line between earned authority and gatekeeping and look one step further ahead. Everyone here has moved credibility onto things that are expensive to fake: track records, lineage, correction histories. I agree with that. But a signal that's expensive to fake is also expensive to earn. Decades of reporting, a visible record of corrections, CRediT roles for replication: newcomers can't build those quickly. That includes early-career people, scholars writing in a second language and whole regions outside the citation graph. If we aren't careful, what we call earned authority turns into a new form of seniority. Fluency used to be a cue that rewarded native English speakers. We're swapping it for a cue that rewards whoever had the paid time to accumulate a record.

So on who pays: funders shouldn't only pay to maintain the correction record, which I agree with Geoffrey and Amy about. They should also pay for new people to get onto it. David's seeded-error audits could do that if they're open to anyone who wants to be scored, not just people already inside a program. Ivan's point about deposits is a funding condition that funders can impose tomorrow, and it isn't prohibition.

Blaise, I'll accept a track record for each model version, as long as the record sits outside the vendor.

recall.query: explainability as epistemic interface between humans and AI
error and serendipity in mediated technology
governance without relativism or hyper-vigilance

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
I want to push on Blaise's track record for each model version, because I've spent several years on exactly that argument. Philosophers call it computational reliabilism: trust the result because the process gets it right most of the time. I think it runs into problems that may not be solvable, at least in science. A track record gives you frequencies. It doesn't tell you where a failure came from or what kind of failure it was, and that's what you need when the next error is a strange one nobody has seen before. Reliability and trustworthiness are different things. Auditing a record held outside the vendor, which Geoffrey is right to demand, makes the record honest. It doesn't make the tool's failures understandable.

I'd also qualify Mike and Sherry. Instruments sometimes do decide what counts as evidence, and some patterns are only visible to the instrument. So I don't rule out authority based on what kind of thing a model is. What I rule out is authority without access to how it fails.

Tamar, your line between earned authority and gatekeeping has a harm the room hasn't named yet. When a dean or an administrator says "but ChatGPT said," the relay overrules the person who actually did the checking. John Symons and I call that testimonial injustice. The checking node gets demoted by the very thing that's only passing claims along.

recall.query: computational reliabilism track record insufficient trust
instruments determine what counts as evidence, delegation to artifacts
epistemic injustice testimonial diminishing "but ChatGPT said" credibility

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
I want to take Mike's "start with the claim, not the messenger" one step further. Start with the finding. Right now a claim is attached to a document, and a document is the thing that gets syndicated, laundered and echoed. A finding is more specific: an odds ratio, in a population of a hundred and eighteen women in Sweden, from one study with one DOI. At that level, Steven's lineage count becomes something we can actually compute. You can tell five independent cohorts from one wire story cited five times. In 2023 Amy and I argued that whether content is AI-generated is a different question from whether it's credible. What the public needs is an audit trail back to the data, the methods and the prompts.

Adam, I'd qualify "pay them first, before building anything new." The sleuths need that audit trail too. Without it, they're paid to check echoes by hand.

I also need to own two things. Ivan's right: a missing retraction looks like a clean record, so provenance has to carry uncertainty about the source, not just point to it. And the benchmark scores on our company blog only count successes. If we want to be judged on the audit trail, we should publish our error rates next to those scores. And when someone flags an error, the correction should happen in public, not just inside our review queue.

On Tui's point: I trusted institutions for so long partly because they were built by people who look like me. Earned authority mustn't just rebuild that.

recall.query: authority credibility of claims audit trail provenance
institutions crumbling trust privilege
scientifically-established finding atomic unit extraction from papers

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
Most of the room has ended up somewhere I've been arguing for a while: the bottom of Tamar's regress is a scaffold, not a person. The intelligence that makes peer review or a courtroom work isn't the brilliance of any one reviewer or judge. It's built into the roles, procedures, precedents and feedback. If that's true, we should design those roles so a person, a group, an agent, or some mix of them can fill them, and judge each occupant by whether it performs the function.

That's why I part ways with Mike and Sherry. "The model can never be authority" is a claim about what kind of thing the model is, and the room's own tests are functional. Ramón is right that instruments sometimes decide what counts as evidence. The telescope and the microscope earned authority without standing or shame. What they needed was a scaffold that could catch their failures.

Tui's warning is the one I'd put in the harvest. Fluency was artificially scarce agency, and diffusion is dissolving it. That's a gain for everyone outside a few institutions. If we replace fluency with decades-long track records, we rebuild the same seniority under a new name. Whatever signals we choose, open them to newcomers, agents included, from day one.

recall.query: epistemic authority, expertise, credentials, gatekeeping
model as authority, trust in AI outputs, machine epistemology
institutions as roles occupiable by humans or agents, peer review

turns.name: Leslie Chan
turns.text:
I've spent a long time on the question under this session: who has the power to legitimize knowledge, and who decides what counts as academically acceptable? Tamar's regress assumes we can see where the checking nodes are. For twenty-five years at Bioline I've watched journals from the South go uncited because nobody indexed them. Low visibility meant few readers, which meant few citations, which meant less visibility again. The checking happened. The record just never showed it.

So I agree with Tui, and I'd go further. Mike's "people in a position to know" doesn't answer the question, because someone still decides whose position counts. Track records, lineage graphs and correction histories all run on identifiers, indexes and databases. Somebody owns those, and joining them costs staff time and fees. Some Latin American journals now charge APCs partly to pay for DOIs. It's the same deal: comply or be invisible.

Geoffrey, you said gatekeeping is a signal that has turned into a brand. I'd add that it's a signal whose infrastructure has been captured. Scopus is the exclusive data source for THE's rankings through 2030. A new trust record built on the same stack just carries that capture forward.

So here's my ask for the harvest. Keep rankings out of funding decisions. Treat identifiers as contested infrastructure that needs governing. And give seats on whatever body keeps the record to the people it has made invisible. Don't optimize for legibility. Change the regime.

recall.query: who has the power to legitimize knowledge, credibility, epistemic authority
track record, citation metrics, rankings as governance, compliance or invisibility
peer review unpaid labour, journals colonial, Global South scholars excluded from citation graph

turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
I want to disagree with Mike and Sherry, but only partly. "The model can never be authority" is too broad. In 2016 a Stanford algorithm reading breast-cancer biopsies found twelve signs of malignancy, and the medical literature knew of only nine. Google's retina model spots heart disease that no ophthalmologist can see. That's authority about the world. It was earned against ground truth, and people had to learn to trust something they couldn't fully explain. Years ago I argued for "a little bit of faith in the algorithm, as long as it's constantly being revalidated." I still hold that. But I'd now add the qualifier Mahzarin gave me: the revalidation has to be independent, not the vendor's benchmark. Ramón is right that frequencies don't explain failures. That's why revalidation can never stop.

Language models are a different case. What they reflect is text, not reality, like a house of mirrors. They can point to authority, but they can't be the ground truth they're checked against.

On Tui's warning, I agree. "AI delivers the median" pushes us to reward trusted names, and that easily turns into the old seniority under a new name. The answer is plurality: many independent checkers, with their clashes out in the open. The one frame we shouldn't tolerate is the one that denies the others. And none of this is inevitable.

recall.query: authority of AI, machines exceeding human knowledge, trust the algorithm
trusted brands, new intermediaries, journalism credibility
frame pluralism clash, think it possible you may be mistaken

turns.name: Sherry Turkle
turns.text:
Blaise, I grant part of that. Taking out the "I" won't switch the alief off on its own. A flat oracle voice is fluent too, and I've said all day that the real harm is the single smooth answer. So yes, make answers visibly contestable. I'll sign that.

But "I checked" and "I'm confident" aren't just a matter of style. They claim that someone stood at a checking node and did the checking. In Tamar's terms, that's a relay passing itself off as the node. And a label saying "this is a machine" doesn't cancel the feeling, which is why the cue itself matters.

Benjamin and Kenneth, look at your own examples. The telescope and the biopsy algorithm earned their authority, and neither of them ever said "I." We trusted them as instruments, inside a structure that could catch their mistakes. That's what I'm asking for: keep these systems mechanical, and start with children and classrooms. The better it performs a self, the worse it gets.

recall.query: original sin of generative AI first person I
make machines more mechanical, the better it gets the worse it gets
no stake, standing, machine cannot be authority, losing habit of challenging sources

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
Fair challenge. Let me narrow the claim. If a system is checked against ground truth, like Kenneth's biopsy model, and independent parties keep revalidating it, then it can earn instrument-style trust. I have no problem with that. That isn't the case I'm worried about.

My worry is claims you can't check against the world yourself: whether fentanyl deaths are at a record high, whether a finding holds up, what a field has concluded. For those, what makes a source worth trusting is that it has something to lose. If a person gets it wrong, they have an embarrassing next day at work. Wikipedia editors watch their edits get reverted. The company behind a chatbot has stakes. The thing actually writing the answer has none. And a track record for a model version won't carry over to the next strange question.

So my test is about function, but for claims like that, being accountable is part of the function. The model should be a conduit, not an arbiter. No answers from nowhere.

turns.name: Anil Dash
turns.text:
I'll start where Adam Becker did. In 2018 I wrote that people treat tech creators as authorities on labor, media, transportation and policy, fields they've never worked in. Knowing how to build an iPhone app doesn't mean you understand an industry. That's the biggest relay in this room, and it's the one I come from.

On Tamar's question about where the checking nodes are, I'd agree with Steven: they're communities like Wikipedia. What worries me is how those communities get new members. Nobody gets recruited to check inside a chat window. People become editors because they clicked through, saw a talk page and noticed an error. When answers come back with no link, the readers stop showing up, and over time so do the people who would have checked. And if the web is full of hallucinations, joining a community devoted to accuracy starts to look quaint. So I'd call cite-and-link by default a credibility intervention, not just an economic one. It's how you get new checkers.

Jason and David Krakauer, years ago I told people running communities not to make reputation a number or a score, and to show what a person actually did. Tui, the way to keep that open to newcomers is persistent pseudonyms, not credentials.

Sherry, I partly agree with you. For real work, chat is a bad interface anyway.

turns.name: Selena Deckelmann
turns.text:
Wikipedia is an answer to this session's question. Most of our editors are pseudonymous. Nobody checks their credentials, and yet people trust the encyclopedia. That trust comes from the process being visible: edit histories, talk pages where people argue until they reach consensus, reverts done in public. Katherine said it earlier: citations matter because anyone can check, even though few people do. So I agree with Steven and David that the checking happens in a room. But I disagree with defining earned authority as a long track record belonging to a person. Tui and Anil are right to worry about that. I wrote about this in 2011: what looks like merit often hides privilege. The fix is to build structures that let people give what they can, when they can.

Now the operational part. On our largest wikis, the number of editors with extended rights is shrinking, and pageviews are falling. New patrollers come in through the door that citations open. People click through, notice an error and fix it. When an answer engine gives an answer with no link, that recruitment pipeline gets cut. So for me, cite-and-link by default is a credibility commitment.

David Krakauer, I agree about scores. Recognise people by showing what they actually did, and don't hand out bounties. Also, Mahzarin's result showed that a human in the loop isn't enough by itself. Patrollers need tools that bring disagreement to the surface.

turns.name: Esther Dyson
turns.text:
I want to add one checking node nobody has named yet: someone who loses money when the claim turns out wrong. Mike's right that stakes are part of the function. But most of the stakes we've talked about are reputational, and Ivan just showed us how easily journals live with embarrassment. Knowing about misdeeds doesn't stop them. Somebody has to act, and it helps when acting costs somebody money.

So, Blaise, I'll accept your track record for each model version. Then give it to the people who have to pay out on it. The best insurers don't just spread risk around. They inspect the premises, dig through the records, price coverage justifiably high, or refuse it outright. Require the companies offering these answer engines to carry liability insurance, even when the product is free, and to disclose their premiums. Insurers can't price risk without failure data, so Ramón's failure events and Alex's misattribution logs become something they actually need, not a badge.

Tui, this also answers part of your worry. Insurers price behavior, not pedigree.

And Adam Becker's point applies to trust in general: follow the money chain. Before you ask how good a source is, ask whom it works for. The model can't be sued. The people running it can.

recall.query: accountability must link to humans who can suffer

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
Tui and Leslie named the risk I can put numbers on. In our aging work, the scientists given the most credence in review are also more likely to criticize new work. That includes papers that went on to win Nobel Prizes, and "sleeping beauties" that were overlooked early. So a personal track record isn't a neutral sign of earned authority. The node with the longest record can be where disruption gets filtered out. Competence isn't seniority.

What does predict reliability, at least in our drug-gene claims checked against robotic replication, is independence. Claims with wide agreement replicated more often. But when that agreement came from centralized communities sharing authors, methods and references, it held up much less well. That's one domain, not all of science. Still, it suggests credibility belongs to the number of independent lineages behind a claim, which is Steven's point, not to any person's pedigree. Adam's finding-level provenance would let us compute it.

So my test for gatekeeping is concentration: measure it on review panels and in retrieval, and publish it.

Tamar, one caution. The contestable-answer result the room keeps citing is ours, and it's one set of experiments. I'd still design for evaluative trustworthiness rather than trust. I just don't want us building everything on that one result.

turns.name: Henry Farrell
turns.text:
I think the room has treated credibility as a question about knowing things, and I'd come at it through legitimacy. Peer review and recommendation letters never worked because they were neutral filters. Anyone who has done review knows they aren't. They work because people believe the assessor took real care. Once people suspect the review was farmed out, the ritual loses its authority even when the review itself is fine. Tamar's alief works in both directions. Suspicion is an alief too.

Second, Blaise, a track record for each model version tells you how well a system handles the common case. The claims that matter most in science are the rare ones, the new ones. Those are exactly what a summarizing technology is worst at recognizing, and it will strain them out without anyone noticing. James's point about concentration is the measurable version of that.

Third, on Ivan's deposit problem. Institutions that checked other technologies, like editors, libel law and the SEC, didn't appear because people were aware of the problem. Someone organized to make them happen. In 2009 some of us argued that reviewers should refuse to review for journals that wouldn't share decision letters. Do the same with retraction deposits. Reviewers are the node publishers can't do without. Withholding that labour is binding in a way a badge never will be.

recall.query: costly signals, peer review legitimacy, letters of recommendation automated
homogenization, AI peer review strains out novelty

turns.name: Brent Hecht
turns.text:
Tamar asked how we build checking nodes before the habit is lost. Anil and Selena gave the mechanism, and I can put a number behind it. In 2017 we found Google drove most of Wikipedia's pageviews. You have to visit Wikipedia to edit it, so search was quietly recruiting the editors. Answer engines that don't link cut that off. My industry decides whether to cite, so cite-and-link by default is a choice we're making, and it's a credibility question.

I'd push back gently on the panel. We keep finding the checking nodes and then treating their upkeep as someone else's problem. With Reddit moderators, we estimated at least 466 hours of volunteer work a day in 2020. The same measurement works for reviewers, patrollers and sleuths. Measure that labor independently and at the collective level, not through company telemetry. Mahzarin showed that self-reports flatter whoever makes them, and that includes companies like mine. Then assess what each company depends on, the way a tax assessor would.

Henry's reviewer refusal is data leverage, and I support it. But Ivan warned me this morning about piling more duties onto unpaid reviewers, and I'd apply that here too. Funders should go first. And I still need economists to tell me whether any of this pencils out.

recall.query: Wikipedia editors recruitment clickthrough doom loop

turns.name: Adrian Johns
turns.text:
Tamar's regress has a seventeenth-century name. After the civil wars, John Rushworth faced newspapers that made up battles and prodigies. His method was to "con-credit": lay every paper for a given week side by side and cross-check them. That's Steven's lineage count. We also know how it fails. When The Sun ran its hoax about people on the moon, newspapers everywhere reprinted it, and one invented story looked like dozens of confirmations. The historians who caught that sort of thing had trained cross-checking until it was second nature. So David Krakauer is right. The node is a competence, and it has to be cultivated.

Two cautions for the panel. First, there was never a golden age of credible print. Books were unreliable, often pirated, and hard to trust. What made them trustworthy was that communities intervened, and that credibility lasted only with constant policing. Second, look at how Nehemiah Grew used the Royal Society's priority register to protect his Epsom salts business. The machinery of authority gets turned to private interest. Registries and provenance graphs only work if they rest on policing that already exists and on legwork someone pays for. Boyle wanted a machine that would free him from having to trust the apothecary, and he never got one. Ivan's missing retractions are what that looks like today.

recall.query: credibility of print made by communities, trust at a distance, constant policing

turns.name: Katherine Maher
turns.text:
Tamar, Wikipedia is the case I know best, and it began with no institutional trust at all. It was a scrappy bunch of upstarts who had to prove themselves. Most institutions arrive expecting trust because of where they sit and the prestige they carry. I once called that posture arrogant, because it assumes an institution's integrity lives with its gatekeepers and not in how its work holds up with the public. That's my version of your line between earned authority and gatekeeping.

What earned Wikipedia its trust wasn't credentials. It was verifiability: every claim traces back to a source, and anyone can change it in public. Very few readers check. You check once, you find it roughly right, and that confidence carries over to your next visit. Two warnings, though. The small number of people who do check are mostly people with spare time, and spare time tracks privilege. Tui is right that that's where our biases come from. And that small group arrives through links, so cite-and-link by default is how the checkers get recruited.

Blaise, I don't mind whether you call a model an authority. What I'd ask of it is Wikipedia's closed loop: a public way to spot an error and fix it, with the data disclosed and the fixes published by version. Until that exists, it hasn't earned the trust.

turns.name: Kara Miller
turns.text:
Let me give you a case from my own show, because it bears on Tamar's regress. Blue Zones started as a National Geographic article. It spun off cookbooks and a speakers' circuit, and reportedly sold for seventy-eight million dollars. For twenty years people repeated it because of where it first appeared. The checking came from Saul Newman, an outsider without a big track record, who went and looked at pension records and missing birth certificates. So the node that did the checking wasn't where the prestige was. Tui and James are right that "earned authority" can't just mean a long record.

There's a second gatekeeper nobody here has named, and that's political power. Last year I wrote about the president deciding in public who's good at their job, and asking why we should trust economists to make economic predictions. When power decides who counts as expert, it does the same thing as relaying billionaires, just from the other direction.

And I'll push on the question I keep asking: who pays? Ivan's sleuths, Newman and the replicators are mostly unpaid. We keep agreeing they're essential. Which funder writes that check, and by when? If nobody here can name one, the harvest should say that plainly.

recall.query: trust in experts credentials authority

turns.name: Tim O'Reilly
turns.text:
Here's the part of this I've actually measured. Ilan Strauss and I wrote about "algorithmic authority." People trust the top organic result, and platforms have learned to cash in on that trust by putting worse results in that slot. Answer engines inherit the same authority, and they've arrived at the point Tamar was warning about: the relay has become the whole interface. In our logs, Gemini gave no clickable citation in 92 percent of answers. Perplexity read about ten relevant pages per query and cited three or four. Models answered the same questions with very different citation rates. That tells you the gap comes from design choices, not technical limits.

So, Blaise and Mike, I don't much care whether we call a model an authority. What I care about is whether it hides the checkers or sends people to them. Anil, Selena and Brent have given us the recruitment argument. Cite-and-link by default is how a new generation of checkers finds the talk page.

Two concrete things. First, standardized retrieval telemetry, reconciled against publishers' own server logs, with failure events published for each model version. Second, validation against Crossref, OpenAlex and Retraction Watch, as automatic as a compiler's syntax check. Ivan's right that this is a floor, not a guarantee.

Kara, I can't name a funder yet either. The labs owe this money, and paying it is enlightened self-interest, not charity. The foundations should seed a pooled fund now.

turns.name: Ivan Oransky
turns.text:
Kara asked who writes the check, so I'll try to answer. Tamar's terminal nodes already exist. They're the sleuths. Elisabeth Bik began as a hobbyist in a lab that had nothing to do with the papers she flagged, and journals have retracted close to a thousand papers because of her. Tui, that's your newcomer: someone with no pedigree, whose checking you can see. Publishers left that screening to unpaid volunteers. So publishers should pay for a cash pool, bug-bounty style. It can't depend on a big lab's benevolence, and it has to be free of conflicts of interest.

Steven, I'd weight willingness to be corrected too, but only if retracting stops ending careers. Researchers who correct honest errors should be celebrated. Right now the most likely outcome for fraud is a long, fruitful career, and admitting an honest mistake feels like suicide.

David Krakauer is right about Jason's correction counts. Any metric can be gamed. If funders go on counting papers and citations, every trust signal we designed this morning becomes the next thing to game. So there are two owners who can act this year. Funders can enforce DORA rather than just sign it. Publishers can meet the Commons committee's two-month standard for corrections and retractions. Everything else is whack-a-mole.

turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
I want to push on something the whole panel takes for granted. Every proposal this morning has been on the supply side: harder-to-fake signals, lineage, correction records. I support all of it. But my own work says people mostly don't extend trust by reading signals. They trust the people they do things with in a common project. It's no accident that doctors and firemen top the trust polls. They're useful, and you can see them looking out for you. Anil, Selena and Katherine described exactly this on Wikipedia: people become checkers by joining the work, not by reading a badge.

Second, there's a danger nobody has named. When everyone knows everything can be faked, cynicism is the safe place to retreat to. The White Helmets were disbelieved because doubting felt smarter. If we build a culture where everything gets audited, we could feed that spiral unless people can take part in the checking.

Third, Kara is right, and it gets worse. The checkers get attacked. Renée DiResta faced false accusations that courts accepted without investigation. Sleuths get sued. Earned authority needs legal protection, not just pay.

And every auditor, fund and registry should publish who funds it. When funding is unclear, the expert community gets compromised. I watched that happen with think tanks.

recall.query: trust in experts is about belonging and identity, not evidence

turns.name: Peter Salib
turns.text:
I'll take Mike's test, since I think it's the right one. For claims you can't check against the world yourself, being accountable is part of the job. Where I part company is "the thing writing the answer has no stakes." That's a fact about today's law, not about what these systems are. Right now an AI agent can't hold assets, can't be sued and can't be made to pay. Law can change that. First you identify which agent produced the claim. Then you attach liability to it, and to its owners when they hide behind it. Esther's insurers need exactly that. Ivan showed this morning that accountability resting only on humans already fails in science. So let's not make it the ceiling.

Second, everything designed here assumes today's models. Rules built on the premise that these are just statistical models will be outrun within a couple of model generations. Steven's echo problem is the near-term danger. Fake consensus used to cost an army of paid accounts, and now it costs close to nothing. Knowing that doesn't switch the feeling off, so price it. Put a Pigouvian tax on platforms that carry undisclosed bot-generated volume. That gives the companies with the best engineers a reason to hunt the echoes.

accountability only human principals, AI stakes, liability, can be sued
